title: SELECT: Choosing Columns & Distinct Values 🎯
description: Retrieve specific columns, use DISTINCT to remove duplicates, and limit result rows.

slides.title: Select Specific Columns 📌
slides.content:
# Move Beyond `SELECT *`

In practice, you rarely need all columns. Specify exactly the columns you want:

```sql
SELECT name, salary FROM employees;
```

This returns only the `name` and `salary` columns. The order of columns in the result matches the order you list them.

You can even reorder columns:
```sql
SELECT salary, name FROM employees;
```

slides.title: Column Selection Example
slides.content: Against our sample data, this would yield:

slides.title: Expected Output 📋
slides.content:
```
name    | department
--------|------------
Alice   | Sales
Bob     | IT
Charlie | Sales
```

quizData.question: What does `SELECT department, name FROM employees;` return?

options.text: The department and name columns, in that order

quizData.explanation: You can choose columns and control their order.

slides.title: Removing Duplicates with `DISTINCT` 🧹
slides.content:
## Only Unique Values

The `DISTINCT` keyword eliminates duplicate rows in the result.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT department FROM employees;
```

This returns:
```
department
----------
Sales
IT
```

Duplicates disappear. You can use `DISTINCT` with multiple columns – then the combination of values must be unique.

quizData.question: What does `SELECT DISTINCT department, salary FROM employees;` return?

options.text: Unique combinations of department and salary

quizData.explanation: `DISTINCT` applies to all selected columns together.

slides.title: Limiting the Number of Rows 🔢
slides.content:
## `LIMIT`

When exploring a large table, you often want only the first few rows:

```sql
SELECT * FROM employees LIMIT 3;
```

In SQLite (and MySQL, PostgreSQL) this returns the first 3 rows. Some databases use `TOP` or `FETCH FIRST`.

You can also skip rows with `OFFSET`:
```sql
SELECT * FROM employees LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1;
```
This skips the first row and returns the next two.

slides.title: LIMIT Example
slides.codeSnippet: SELECT name, salary FROM employees LIMIT 2;

quizData.question: What does `LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10` do?

options.text: Skips the first 10 rows and returns the next 5 rows

quizData.explanation: `OFFSET` skips rows, `LIMIT` restricts count after offset.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use `LIMIT` to Test Queries

When developing complex queries, always add `LIMIT` to avoid accidentally returning millions of rows and freezing your tool.

slides.title: Try It: Column Selection 🏋️
slides.content:
1. Write a query to show only `name` and `department` from `employees`.
2. Write a query to display all unique departments.
3. Write a query that returns the first 3 employees, ordered by whatever (we haven’t learned ordering yet; just LIMIT will do).

Use the sample table structure: id, name, department, salary.

slides.title: Column Control Done! 🎉
slides.content: Now you can pick exactly the data you want. Next, we’ll filter rows with conditions.
